thread.title: What The Apple HomePod Means For AAPL Investors

author: Martin Tillier
title: What The Apple HomePod Means For AAPL Investors
text:
HomePod (Photo courtesy of Apple)
This morning, we learned that the Apple ( AAPL ) HomePod will be available to order Friday, with an expected delivery date of February 9. The HomePod is the Cupertino giant’s home speaker system, their answer to Amazon ( AMZN )’s Echo and Google ( GOOGL )’s Home. We knew it was coming and, based on history, now that it is here we know what the reactions will be.
The doubters will point out that Apple is late to the party. They will state with absolute certainty that the HomePod, due to its delayed entry into the market, will fail terribly, and could be the beginning of the end of Apple. Many, including many investors and analysts who should know better, will believe them, and AAPL will probably underperform for a while as a result.
Students of the company’s history, however, will use that weakness as an opportunity to load up on stock in what is arguably the most successful company in the history of the world.
What the doubters forget is that we have been through this many times before, and each time those that maintain that Apple has made a mistake have been proven wrong. Re-making an existing product, or expanding on an idea, is what Apple has been doing for years, and they do it better than anybody else. They don’t steal ideas, they improve on them.
Think of the watch, years after Fitbit ( FIT ) and Samsung Gear, or the move towards larger phones, or any one of a host of things dating back to the release of the iPhone when Blackberry ( BB ) dominated the smartphone market, or even to the launch of the original Macs to compete with PCs.
It has happened so many times that it can no longer be viewed as a problem but rather as a deliberate strategy. Why not let others innovate and wait until the glitches and security problems become apparent before stepping in? Why not wait until consumers have expressed their preferences for improvements to what is available?
Conventional wisdom holds that once a brand is established in a consumer product, the “first mover” advantage is substantial, but in the case of Apple it doesn’t apply, mainly for one good reason. Everything we do these days seems to flow through our phones, and the iPhone dominates the smart phone market almost to the point of ubiquity. The prospect of seamless integration of any home speaker system with the computers in our pockets is an enormous advantage for Apple, and one that will make the HomePod a success, late entry notwithstanding.
So, what should potential or existing investors do? It will probably pay to wait for a while. There will almost inevitably be an initial period of negativity among reviewers and users. Those that find fault will be motivated to comment, while the vast majority of users who integrate the HomePod into their daily lives will remain silent. That is just a product of human nature, but the negative vibes will, if history is any guide, hold AAPL back.
That will be the time to buy the stock, whether as a short-term trade or to add to existing holdings, because eventually, as with all the other products, the real story will become clear after a few months of sales. The HomePod is neither groundbreaking nor particularly innovative, but it will probably follow the pattern of other Apple products and add to the company’s massive revenue and profits. So, Apple-haters and doubters, bring on the negativity. That way, the rest of us can buy the stock at a discount.
